title: Accessible names and labels for screen readers
when: Controls, icons, images or links are announced badly or not at all by screen readers, or forms lack labels.
prompt:
Goal: Every control, image and landmark has a short, accurate accessible name and fields carry their hints and errors.
Steps:
1. Form fields: a visible <label for> per input; group radios and checkboxes in fieldset with legend.
2. Hints and errors: link with aria-describedby; set aria-invalid="true" on fields with errors.
3. Icon only buttons get aria-label naming the action (Delete invoice 42), and the inner svg gets aria-hidden="true".
4. Images: alt describes the content and purpose; decorative images get alt=""; charts get a text summary.
5. Links: text that makes sense alone; repeated "Read more" gets context with visually hidden text.
6. Name landmarks when repeated: two nav elements get aria-label="Main" and aria-label="Footer".
Quality bar:
- Names match the visible text where there is one.
- Names are short and start with the key word.
- No redundant words like "button" or "image of".
Pitfalls:
- Placeholder used as the only label.
- aria-label on a div with no role, which is ignored.
- Alt text that repeats the file name.
Verify:
- [ ] Every input has a label.
- [ ] Every img has alt.
- [ ] Links have meaningful text.
- [ ] Inline SVGs have a title or aria-hidden.
Output: Updated HTML with labels, names and descriptions, and a visually-hidden utility class in CSS if needed.

examples.input: o leitor de tela fala só "botão" nos ícones
examples.output: aria-label="Edit task" and "Delete task" on icon buttons, svg aria-hidden, labels for 6 inputs
